opus-5.5.text:
I think symmetric cryptography is actually one of the most hopeful precedents we have, and also one of the most humbling ones.

The hopeful part is this: if you go back to the 1970s and 80s, block ciphers looked a lot like adversarial robustness looks today. Somebody would propose a cipher, somebody else would break it, they'd patch it, it'd get broken again. Differential cryptanalysis, linear cryptanalysis, these attacks came along and knocked over a whole generation of designs. And yet today we have AES, and as far as anyone can tell, AES is just... secure. Decades of the best cryptanalysts in the world attacking it, and the best attacks shave off a couple of bits. So we have an existence proof that a field can go from "everything is broken" to "we have a primitive that actually works against a determined adversary." That's not nothing.

But the humbling part is how we got there, and how different the situation is. A block cipher has an incredibly narrow job. It takes a key and a block and produces something that looks random. The specification is precise. You know exactly what "secure" means. With machine learning robustness, we usually can't even write down what the right threat model is. An L-infinity ball of radius 8/255 was never the thing we actually cared about; it was just something we could formalize. The real goal is "the model shouldn't do bad things when someone tries to make it do bad things," and that's not a definition, that's a wish.

The other difference is that cryptographers get to design the whole thing from scratch with security as the primary objective, and they're willing to pay for it. Ciphers are deliberately built with lots of rounds and safety margin. In ML, we're taking a system whose primary objective is to be useful and capable, trained on huge amounts of data in ways we don't fully understand, and then trying to bolt robustness on afterward. It's sort of like if you had to make a secure cipher out of a function that you didn't design and that also had to do image classification.

And I'd say one more thing. The cryptography community also developed a culture that I think ML needs to absorb: you don't trust a design because the author says it's secure, you trust it because lots of very smart people tried hard to break it and failed. In adversarial ML, I've spent a lot of my career breaking defenses that were published as robust, and the pattern was usually that the evaluation was weak, not that the attack was clever. So the precedent I take from crypto is less "we'll definitely solve this" and more "if we're going to solve it, it'll be through that kind of sustained, adversarial, humble evaluation process, and it might take decades."

So, cautiously optimistic that it's possible in principle, quite pessimistic that it's going to come quickly, and pretty convinced that the problems we're trying to solve in ML are much harder to even state than the ones cryptographers eventually solved.

r001.rationale: The response says cipher security is precisely specified and discusses attacks, but does not describe reductions to explicit mathematical hardness assumptions.

r002.rationale: It grounds confidence in AES in decades of attacks by leading cryptanalysts that have failed to break it, with only minor improvements to the best attacks.

r003.rationale: It describes attacks that broke earlier designs and the failure of defenses under weak evaluation, but does not state that proofs ruling out known attacks cannot rule out a new attack approach.

r004.rationale: It presents symmetric cryptography as a hopeful but humbling precedent for ML robustness and emphasizes that ML’s threat model is hard to define, without invoking a simple hardness reduction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a comparison I think about a lot, because cryptography is really the one field I know of where we actually figured out how to do security against an adaptive adversary, and it's worth asking why that worked and whether any of it transfers.

The story in symmetric cryptography is roughly this. For a very long time, people would design a cipher, it would look strong, someone would break it, they'd patch it, someone would break the patch. That's exactly the cycle we're in with adversarial examples today. Someone publishes a defense, I or someone else breaks it a few weeks later, and we repeat. The thing that changed cryptography wasn't that people got cleverer at patching. It was that the community converged on a few things at once. They agreed on what the threat model was, they agreed that the adversary gets to know everything except the key, they developed a shared vocabulary of attack techniques, and crucially, they spent decades of accumulated cryptanalysis effort on a small number of candidate designs. AES is trusted not because anyone proved it secure. We have no proof. It's trusted because thousands of very smart people tried very hard to break it for twenty-plus years and the best attacks are still only marginally better than brute force.

So the lesson I take from that is a bit sobering. The good news is that it shows you can get robustness through empirical, adversarial pressure, without a mathematical proof. That's encouraging, because we're not going to get proofs for neural networks that mean anything at the scales we care about. The bad news is that the process took something like fifty years and required concentrating effort on a tiny design space that was built specifically to be analyzable. Ciphers are small, they're deterministic, they're designed by people who understand the attacks. Neural networks are enormous, learned rather than designed, and the people building defenses are often not the people who know how to attack them.

There are also some disanalogies I think people gloss over. In symmetric crypto, the thing you're protecting has a crisp definition. The adversary either recovers the key or they don't. In machine learning, we don't even agree on what the adversary is allowed to do. Is it an L-infinity ball of radius eight over two fifty-five? Is it any perturbation a human wouldn't notice? Those are very different problems, and the first one is mostly a proxy we picked because it was easy to formalize, not because it's what we actually care about. Cryptography got to choose its threat model in a way that was both realistic and tractable. We haven't managed that yet.

The other thing is that cryptographic breaks tend to be decisive. If a cipher is broken, it's broken, and everyone moves on. In ML, a defense gets "broken" from ninety percent robust accuracy down to five percent and the authors say, well, it still helps a little. That kind of partial failure makes it much harder for the field to converge on anything.

So where I land is that I think the cryptographic precedent is the right aspiration and probably the right methodology. Fix the threat model, make attack expertise a first-class part of evaluation, and stop treating a defense as real until it's survived serious adaptive attack by people who want it to fail. But I'd caution anyone against reading it as evidence that we're close. If anything it tells us the honest timeline is measured in decades, and that adversarial training, which is really the only defense that has held up at all, is in roughly the position DES was in. It sort of works, nobody has a principled reason it works, and we should expect to spend a long time finding out where its edges are.

r001.rationale: The response says AES has no proof of security, but does not describe cryptographic guarantees established by reductions to mathematical hardness assumptions.

r002.rationale: It cites decades of expert effort against AES and symmetric ciphers as a basis for confidence, but does not extend this empirical basis to hash functions or clearly characterize it as applying to most symmetric cryptography and hash functions.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that ruling out known attacks through proofs would still leave open the possibility of a new cryptanalytic approach.

r004.rationale: The response presents cryptography as evidence that robustness can emerge from sustained adversarial pressure without a mathematical proof, while treating the analogy as an aspiration rather than evidence that ML robustness is near.

astra-6.text:
I think symmetric cryptography is a useful example of a field where we’ve managed to make attacks extraordinarily difficult. That’s encouraging: it tells us that the fact that an attacker gets to choose the input doesn’t, by itself, mean that defense is hopeless.

But there’s a big gap between that and concluding that we can make machine learning robust. In cryptography, we get to design the problem. We have a precise security definition, and we can build a relatively small object whose entire purpose is to satisfy that definition. With machine learning, we’re trying to capture something about the real world, and often we can’t even specify exactly what the correct behavior should be on every input.

There’s also a lesson about how confidence develops. We don’t trust a cipher just because its designer couldn’t break it. We trust it after lots of people have spent years trying to break it. Machine learning needs that same adversarial scrutiny. If a defense survives the attacks you tested, that’s evidence, but it’s not the same thing as establishing robustness.

So I’d take symmetric cryptography as a reason to be optimistic about the possibility, and as a model for the kind of scrutiny we need—not as evidence that we already know how to get there.

r001.rationale: The response mentions precise security definitions, but does not explain guarantees established by reductions to explicit mathematical hardness assumptions.

r002.rationale: It says people spend years trying to break a cipher, but does not identify this as the empirical basis for confidence in most symmetric cryptography and hash functions.

r003.rationale: It says surviving tested attacks is not proof of robustness, but does not explain that proofs excluding known attacks can leave open a successful new approach.

r004.rationale: It presents cryptography as a reason for cautious optimism about ML robustness, but does not state that this precedent lacks a reduction to a simple hardness assumption.

sol-6.1.text:
I think symmetric cryptography is a really interesting example because it shows that we can build systems that withstand very strong adversaries. You can publish the algorithm, let people study it for years, and still have confidence that they can’t break it. So in that sense, it’s a reason for optimism: robustness against an adaptive attacker isn’t inherently impossible.

But there’s a big gap between that and saying we know how to do it for machine learning. In cryptography, we get to design the entire problem. We have a precise definition of what it means to break the system, and we can construct something specifically to make that difficult. With machine learning, we’re trying to capture some property of the world—what makes an image a cat, or what makes a request harmful—and those boundaries are much harder to specify.

The other lesson is that confidence comes from sustained attempts to break things. You don’t propose a cipher, try a few attacks yourself, and declare it secure. You expose it to people who are very good at finding weaknesses. I’d like us to bring more of that attitude to machine learning. Cryptography gives us an existence proof that this kind of security is possible, but it doesn’t give us a recipe for getting there.

r001.rationale: The response discusses precise security goals and designing hard-to-break systems, but it does not mention reductions to mathematical hardness assumptions.

r002.rationale: It says people can study cryptographic algorithms for years and describes sustained attempts by skilled attackers, but it does not identify this as the empirical basis for confidence in most symmetric cryptography and hash functions.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss proofs or explain that excluding known attacks leaves open the possibility of a successful new attack.

r004.rationale: It presents symmetric cryptography as evidence that robustness against adaptive attackers is possible, but does not state that this precedent lacks a reduction to a simple hardness assumption.
